chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
title: Rehearsals and the Apollo Theater audition with Jelly Roll
summary: Caldwell recalls rehearsals and an audition for Mr. Schiffman at the Apollo where Jelly Roll insisted on playing his new number and lost the job.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: So what happened, I'll never forget, (unintelligible) and I were Apollo (unintelligible) good friends. We rehearsed two weeks in the Parlor Theater. So --
This was in 19- -- this was after -- just before the war.
Oh, that's around the time you recorded with him.

Yeah, 1939. We recorded it on the (unintelligible) recording. So Jelly, (unintelligible) was (unintelligible) right next to where I lived at 209, because the house I lived in, Jelly lived in for years, so Jelly said, well, we going to have an audition with Mr. Schiffman down at the Apollo Theater. All right, Jelly, Johnny. So we got the thing together. Jelly Johnny had a few numbers, said, Hap, got a new number, (unintelligible). I said, well, what is it, Jelly Johnny? "Finger Buster" -- Jelly Johnny got on there with who-woo-wump. I said, Johnny, that's fine.

He was experienced. So we got the thing together, said, we're going to make this audition. We'll make it down at the Apollo Parlor Theater, the (unintelligible) rehearsal hall downstairs next door. We got down there, got everything set up. David Nelson's trumpet player. He's a nephew of Joe Oliver Geronimo, yeah. He's from New Orleans too. So we got down there, we played some numbers, and Mr. Shipley said, that's fine, gentlemen.

Good. That's all we wanted, said, no, wait a minute. Got another number. Mr. Shipman said, I don't want to hear no more numbers. Get that thing over, Jelly. Mr. Schiffman Shipman, you've got to hear. This is my new number, "Finger Buster." So Dave looked at me, I said (unintelligible) let him alone. He got to fooling with the "Finger Buster" and lost the job, and we gave him hell. So he (unintelligible).
